title: Yelp can now call on your behalf to check wait times at a restaurant
content:
Over the last few weeks, personal assistants like Instinct, Fo, and Muse have enabled users to call businesses for customer support and appointment booking. Following this trend, Yelp is adding the ability for its app users to get a voice agent to call a restaurant to check wait times.
The new feature, Check for Me, will show up on restaurant pages in the app, where users can enter their party size and phone number. The AI agent then calls on behalf of the user to check wait times and texts them the results to decide if they want to go to that particular restaurant.
Last year, Yelp debuted its voice solution for restaurants and service providers. With this new feature, the discovery platform is fulfilling the consumer side of the equation, though there is a possibility that a user’s agent will talk to the restaurant’s agent, and agent-to-agent communication might break down the conversation.
The company is also updating its Yelp AI assistant that helps users discover restaurants and services. With the new OpenTable integration, users can easily book a restaurant without leaving the app.
Yelp is adding better personalization to its assistant by having it remember preferences that you might have mentioned in previous chats. Plus, you can access your chat history from the past 30 days in the app, with full history available soon.
Users can ask the chatbot to set custom reminders, such as sending suggestions for weekend activities every Friday. The company is also letting users build their own lists, starting with two “Been Here” and “Want to
Go” lists. You can filter your lists by location, category, and cuisine, reorder, add notes to items, and share them with others. 
Next month, the company will start showing weekly personalized recommendations based on your saved items and rankings. Yelp is also working on converting collections to lists and giving the lists tab a new look, rolling out later in the year, along with a maps view.
To cap off all these changes, Yelp has been thinking about enhancing customer support and business processes through AI. In the new update, the company is releasing a new paid product called Smart Lead Reply, which can reply to customers and engage with them to qualify a lead. Business owners, who will be charged $30 per month for these services, can specify how an agent should handle a conversation with a customer. Other companies like Meta have also been courting small businesses with AI offerings to handle inbound customer inquiries.

report.summary: Yelp’s new Check for Me feature lets an AI voice agent call restaurants for wait times, text results back, and supports booking via OpenTable and a more personalized assistant.
report.background: Yelp is a discovery platform built around restaurant and local-service reviews, but it has increasingly moved into transactions and AI-assisted workflows. Last year, Yelp launched a voice solution for restaurants and service providers, mainly to handle inbound calls. Now it is extending that capability to consumers, following a wave of personal assistants such as Instinct, Fo, and Muse that can call businesses for support and appointments. The broader context is the rapid maturation of speech-based AI agents: large language models, real-time speech recognition, and telephony APIs now make automated calls practical, though reliability and agent-to-agent communication remain open questions. Yelp is also broadening its assistant into booking, personalization, reminders, and small-business lead management.
key_points: Check for Me appears on restaurant pages in the Yelp app. Users enter party size and phone number, and an AI voice agent calls the restaurant to ask about wait times. Yelp then texts the result back so the user can decide whether to go.

The feature has a notable technical wrinkle: Yelp already offers voice agents to restaurants, so a user’s AI agent may end up talking to the restaurant’s AI agent. Yelp acknowledges that agent-to-agent conversations might break down, raising questions about reliability and natural handoff.

Yelp’s assistant is getting broader. An OpenTable integration lets users book restaurants without leaving the app, while new memory features remember preferences from past chats. Users can access 30 days of chat history, set custom reminders, and build shareable lists such as Been Here and Want to Go.

Yelp is also monetizing AI for businesses with Smart Lead Reply, a $30-per-month product that replies to customers and qualifies leads. Business owners can specify how the agent should handle conversations, putting Yelp in competition with platforms like Meta that are courting small businesses with AI customer-service tools.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Yelp’s move shows consumer voice agents shifting from demos into mainstream local-commerce workflows. Success will depend less on flashy conversation and more on latency, call reliability, consent, and clean escalation when agents talk to agents or humans. Developers get a clear signal that telephony orchestration, structured handoffs, booking APIs, and CRM integrations are becoming core building blocks. For regular users, the appeal is convenience: fewer calls and faster answers. But it also raises privacy concerns around phone numbers, accuracy risks when wait times change, and the possibility of automated call spam burdening restaurants. Agent-to-agent protocols and clear disclosure will matter.
report.tools: To follow: Yelp Check for Me and the updated Yelp AI assistant; OpenTable for in-app booking; comparable consumer-call agents Instinct, Fo, and Muse. Developers exploring similar voice-call agents can watch LiveKit Agents, Vocode, Twilio Programmable Voice, and OpenAI’s Realtime API for telephony, speech-to-text, and text-to-speech orchestration, while respecting consent and call-recording rules.
